chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Saif ibn 'Amirah, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the sick person in the month of Ramadan who does not recover until he dies; he said: 'His fasts are not made up for him.' And about the menstruating woman who dies in the month of Ramadan; he said: 'Her fasts are not made up for her.'

The explanation in these hadiths is that making up the fasts for the deceased is only obligatory if he had recovered from his illness and neglected making up what was missed of his prayer and fasting; then it becomes obligatory upon his guardian to make it up for him. But if he died while in that illness, it is not obligatory upon anyone to make it up for him. And that which indicates what we mentioned is what he narrated:

key_terms.الْحَائِضُ: The menstruating woman, whose menstruation is a valid excuse for not fasting.
key_terms.الْقَضَاءُ: Making up missed obligatory acts (e.g., fasting or prayer) after their time has passed.
key_terms.الْمَرِيضُ: The sick person, specifically one whose illness prevented fasting.
key_terms.الْوَلِيُّ: The guardian or heir responsible for fulfilling the deceased's obligations.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for making up missed Ramadan fasts if a person dies before recovering from their illness or menstruation?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the Shia juristic distinction between death during the impediment versus after recovery, establishing that *qada'* (making up) is not obligatory if the deceased died while still in the state of illness or menstruation. This ruling underscores the principle that the obligation to compensate for missed acts is tied to the individual's capacity and prior neglect, rather than being an automatic transfer to the heir. The commentary highlights that the guardian's duty arises only when the deceased had the opportunity to fulfill the obligation but failed to do so before passing.
